english: Two armies were standing facing each other. Then the Strong One stepped forward and cried out: 'Which man will come against me? My hand killed ten. My fame is great.' Then the High One (Bherghonts) said: 'Strong One, I will come against you.' The High One lifted up his two hands: 'Father Sky, hear me. Give me power.' Then the Strong One's spear went astray. The High One struck the Strong One's heart with a spear. Then the Strong One sank to the ground and grew cold. The High One's army rejoiced, and the Strong One's army [we] went away. Then the High One, having seized the Strong One's spear, carried it to his father. He (the father) said to him: 'Great is your fame, and the Strong One's fame is yours too.'
uncertain: bʰérǵʰonts: adjective 'high' used as a personal name (or participle 'rising')
ḱuh₁rós: adjective 'strong' used as a name/epithet

misfit: gʷh₂mé: AOR.1PL 'we went' but the subject in its clause is ḱuh₁rósyo kóryos (3SG); expected gʷéh₂t 'it went'

english: The father-in-law was cooking beef. Udros (Otter) and Bherghus (High) were sitting around the fire, drinking mead, and the two became drunk. Then Bherghus spoke: 'Udros, your hand is weak (light) and your heart trembles.' Udros stood up and said: 'Bherghus, my hand is not weak. Let us two fight it out!' Then the father-in-law stood between them and said: 'Udros and Bherghus, do not fight, you two. You two are drunk. A guest is dear to the host. Lie down, you two.' Then the two lay down. At dawn the two woke, and Udros gave Bherghus a spear, and Bherghus gave Udros two horses. Then they were content (sated).
uncertain: udrós / bʰérǵʰus: adjectives ('aquatic, otter' / 'high') treated as personal names
gʷṓs pékʷet: 'cattle' ACC.PL; read as cooking beef
h₁ln̥gʷʰrós: 'lightweight', taken as 'weak'
h₁éǵʰs powǵéyōwos: SBJV.1DU 'let us two fight', h₁éǵʰs 'out' (outside / to the end)
sh₂ént: 3PL 'they became sated' though only two men are in focus; may include the father-in-law

english: The Sheep and the Horses

english: Markos (the Horse) was living by the river. Men could not overcome him, and he kept breaking chariots. Then Dlh₁ghos (Long) went carrying honey and sat down at the river. Markos came and [they] were licking the honey. Long grabbed his head. Markos trembled and sweated. Then Long spoke to him: 'Markos, do not be afraid. I will not kill you.' Markos grew used to Long. Then Long yoked him to the chariot and drove to his own father. The father was astonished and said: 'You have overcome Markos. You will overcome men, and your fame will be imperishable.'
uncertain: dl̥h₁gʰós: adjective 'long' used as a personal name
déh₂nu: endingless form, read as LOC 'at the river' (could be ACC 'to the river')
térh₂us: PST.2SG of a present stem, read as 'you overcame'
misfit: liǵʰént: PST.3PL 'they were licking', but the subject is márkos (SG) coordinated with gʷémt 3SG; expected léyǵʰt

english: Then the king approached the god Werunos, (in order) now to worship the god.

sesole: perfect of 'jump'; with úpo read as 'went up to, approached'

h₃rḗḱs: spelling variant of h₃rḗǵs (non-standard orthography in this text)

english: The wolf and two brothers made a pact. The wolf said: 'Father Sky, listen to my word. I will not steal the brothers' cattle. If I steal them, may Perkunos strike me.' In spring the wolf saw the brothers' cattle in the field. When it was getting dark he drove them to his own stall. At dawn the two brothers were searching for the cattle. The two tracked them to his stall and said: 'Wolf, you have been breaking the pact.' He said: 'I was not stealing them.' Then the clouds were coming, and Perkunos struck the wolf with fire. The wolf fell, and his stall burned. The cattle came out of it, and the two brothers drove them to the field. Whoever breaks a pact, Perkunos strikes him.
uncertain: wésni: LOC of wósr̥ 'in spring' or wósn̥ 'for sale'; spring chosen
nébʰōs: NOM/ACC.PL neuter 'clouds'; taken as subject of gʷm̥sḱét (neuter plural with singular verb)

sth₂dʰlóm h₁éwseto: MID 'burned (intr.)'
misfit: bʰréh₂tēr: NOM.SG after dwóh₁ 'two'; expected dual bʰréh₂terh₁ (as used later in the same text)

english: The free man's (Leudheros') daughter was tending sheep in the field. When it was getting dark, a wolf came. The sheep trembled. The daughter lifted the burning fire and went at him. She burned his head. Trembling, the wolf went away. Then Leudheros heard the news and said: 'Daughter, you have protected the sheep. I will give you a name, and it will be famous.' Then he gave the daughter a dog, and the dog guarded them (the sheep) together with her.
uncertain: h₁léwdʰeros: adjective 'free' used as a name
dʰégʷʰont: neuter participle 'burning' agreeing with péh₂wr̥
tósyo káput h₁éwset: active 'she burned his head'
wékʷos: 'word', read as 'the news'
tā́s: FEM ACC.PL referring back to h₂ówins (f.)

english: A spear wounded Wesus (the Good). Wesus fell from the chariot and lay on the ground. His brother arrived and lifted him in his hands. Wesus spoke: 'Brother, my death has come. Lead my horses to my mother, and let [him] tell her: "Your son did not fear death."' Then he died. The brother carried him to the mother by chariot. She saw him and cried out, and her tears were flowing: 'Dear son, you lie on the ground. You will not see the dawn, and you will not drive the swift horses. Your fame will not perish.' Then they laid him on the fire, and the brother spoke to Agni (Fire): 'Agni, carry my brother to the gods.' Then the fire burned him. Men remember his imperishable fame.
uncertain: h₁wésus: adjective 'good' used as a name
kʷékʷloh₁: INS.SG 'by chariot' (could be DU)

english: Ph₃tos (the Drunk) was drinking mead and killed a man. That man had a brother. The brother heard the news and his heart grew hot: 'I will not eat and I will not drink; I will find him.' Then the brother, grasping a spear, followed him. The Drunk went to a high hill and lay down in sleep. The brother climbed it and found the Drunk lying there. Then he cried out: 'Drunk, wake up! I am the brother of the man whom you killed.' Then the Drunk woke, stood up and trembled. Then the brother pierced his heart with the spear, and the Drunk died. Then he drank mead and rejoiced, and his fame was imperishable.
uncertain: ph₃tós: participle 'drunk' used as a name
bʰréh₂tēr tósmey h₁ést: 'to him (the slain man) was a brother'; tósmey could also refer to the Drunk

ḱéym̥h₁nom: middle participle 'lying', agreeing with ph₃tóm

english: The army was making ready. Then the mother of Lewbhos (the Dear one) said to him: 'My son, two paths lie before you. If you enter the battle, you will die, and your fame will be imperishable. If you stay sitting with your father, you will live, and men will not hear your name.' Lewbhos said: 'Mother, I will enter the battle. A man dies; fame does not die.' Then the mother's heart trembled. She clothed him in wool and gave him a spear. Then Lewbhos drove the chariot forward. The mother stood on a hill and watched him. Death seized Lewbhos, and his fame did not die.
uncertain: lewbʰós: adjective 'dear' used as a name
h₂réydʰeto: MID 'was arranging itself, getting ready'
ph₂tréh₁: INS 'with (your) father' (péh₂tōr 'protector' also possible)
mért: AOR used gnomically 'dies'

english: Keh₂ilos (the Whole) woke. It grew light. He stood up and spoke to Dawn: 'Dawn, daughter of Sky, hear my word. I am going into battle. Ten warriors stand against me. May I see your light.' Dawn heard him. Then Keh₂ilos went into the battle and killed nine warriors. Then a spear wounded him. Keh₂ilos was lying on the ground, and the sun set. It was getting dark. Then dawn broke, and Keh₂ilos saw her light and died. The daughter of Sky cried out.
uncertain: kéh₂ilos: adjective 'healthy, whole' used as a name
léwkt, h₁regʷesyét, h₂wést: impersonal weather/light verbs

english: The woman's husband fell in battle. Her brother-in-law carried him by chariot. The woman saw him, cried out, and beat her breast. 'Husband, you lie there. You do not look at the sun. You do not listen to my word. Who will protect me? Who will tend the sheep?' The brother-in-law spoke: 'Woman, do not be afraid. I will protect you and the sheep.' Then the two built a fire and laid him on it. The fire burned him, and his radiance went up to the sky. The brother-in-law set his spear upright on the hill and said: 'May men see it and remember his name. His fame will be imperishable.'
uncertain: kʷékʷloh₁: INS.SG 'by chariot' (could be DU)

english: Enemies seized the brothers' sister and were leading her into their own fortress. The fortress was high, and its wall was long. The two brothers came to the wall and cried out: 'Sister, are you alive?' The sister heard them and said: 'I am alive. They are guarding me.' When it was getting dark, the two climbed the wall. They (the enemies) were lying asleep. Then the brothers saw the sister and freed her. The lord of the fortress woke and followed the two. The two stood against him at the ford and killed him. Then the sister swam across the river with the brothers, and their father rejoiced, and their fame is imperishable.
uncertain: bʰréh₂tr̥bʰis: INS.PL 'with the brothers' for two brothers (no dual oblique form available)

english: The lord died. Then the brother set up ten cattle on the hill and said: 'Whoever wins, to him I will give the cattle.' Then Swekuros (the brother-in-law) yoked two horses to a chariot, and H₁lengʷhros (the Light one) yoked two horses to a chariot. Then the two drove the swift horses around the hill. Then the brother-in-law's horse slipped, and his chariot broke. The brother-in-law fell down to the ground and his two hands were cut, and the Light one passed him. The Light one's horses were sweating, and the Light one reached the cattle. Then the brother said: 'Light one, you have won. Take the cattle.' He gave the brother-in-law two sheep and said: 'Brother-in-law, your horses are swift. Take two sheep.' And the Light one's name became famous.
uncertain: swēḱurós: 'brother-in-law', possibly a name here
h₁ln̥gʷʰrós: adjective 'light(weight)' used as a name

dʰégʷʰh₂t: 'came near, passed by'
gʷṓs: ACC as goal 'reached the cattle'

english: The son-in-law was standing on the stronghold and watching the river. He saw enemies coming along the river, and they were driving chariots. He went down to the king and said: 'King, enemies are coming with chariots.' The king said: 'Let us stand at the ford and hide ourselves.' Then they hid at the ford. The enemies reached the ford, and the chariots went into the water. Then they (the king's men) rose up and struck them with spears. The water was red. The chariots broke and sank in the water. The king took their horses and gave them to the son-in-law, and said: 'Son-in-law, you were watchful. Your fame is good.'

english: Death took the lord of the swift horses. The horses stood by the chariot and would not go into battle. They put their heads down to the ground, and their tears were flowing. Men drove them on, but they did not move. Then Father Dyeus saw them and said: 'Horses, death has not taken you; death has taken men. Go into battle. Carry your lord's chariot.' Then he gave them strength. Then the horses moved and carried the chariot forward. People remember it.

uncertain: wēlh₁si: root 'choose/want', long-grade spelling not in lexicon; 'what do you wish/choose'

english: H₃reǵtos (the Upright) lived by the ford, and his daughter was milking the cows. Then a stranger arrived, and he was tired. The Upright seated him by the fire, and she brought him a washbasin. He cooked a sheep for him and gave him mead and water. He (the guest) ate and drank. Then he said: 'Upright one, you have been giving me good things. I am a god. I am seeking what is right. ' The Upright was astonished. The god said: 'Do not be afraid. May your sheep increase, and may your daughter find a good husband.' Then the god went up to the sky, and the Upright's sheep increased. His daughter met a good husband in spring, and his good fame became great.

english: The father went away. His son grew up, became a warrior, and grew strong in his youth. Then the father arrived with an army, and the warrior went against him. 'Warrior, who is your father?' 'My father went away. Men say he perished.' 'I am your father.' 'I do not trust you. Lift your spear.' Then he said: 'Either I will kill my son, or the son will kill me.' Then the two fought. The father's spear pierced his heart. The warrior fell to the ground and said: 'Now I know you, father.' Then he died. He (the father) cried out and lay down beside him. 'Your fame will be imperishable. May death take me.'

speaker assignment of the dialogue lines is inferred

english: It was getting dark. Two warriors came to the Upright's field, and his cattle were standing over there. The dogs were lying asleep. Then the two seized the cattle and drove them away. Then it grew light. The Upright woke and did not see his cattle, and his heart grew hot. He cried out and spoke to his sons: 'Yoke the swift horses to the chariot, you two. Let us follow the two men who drove off our cattle.' Then they climbed onto the chariot and drove the horses on. They tracked the cattle. Then they saw the two at the ford. Trembling, the two let the cattle go and swam across the water. The two sons killed the two with spears. Then the Upright drove the cattle to the field, and men heard of his great fame. He gave a sheep to the gods at the place of worship.

english: Cattle and horses were in the stable. When death took the father, the two brothers were dividing the cattle. The elder said: 'The horses shall be mine, and the cattle shall be yours.' Leudheros (the Free one) said: 'The horses shall not be yours,' and he raised his hand against his brother. Then their mother came between them and said: 'Brothers, do not fight, you two. Your father watches you two from the sky. Let the elder take the horses, and let Leudheros take the cattle, and let the two of you make a pact at the fire.' The two listened to their mother. They made a pact and drank, and the mother rejoiced.

english: The king was travelling on the sea for ten years. Then he arrived at his land. He was wearing wool and covering his head, and the men did not recognize him. That dog of his was lying in the stable. The dog saw him, recognized him and licked his hand. Then the dog grew cold (died). He went to his wife. Ten men were sitting there and ate his cattle. The woman said to him: 'Who are you?' 'I am your husband. I have arrived.' She said to him: 'If you are my husband, tell me your father's [names (DAT/ABL.PL)].' Then he spoke his own father's famous name, and the woman recognized him and rejoiced. Then he seized a spear and killed those ten men. Then he sat with her, and his fame became good.

h₁dént: 'ate' (AOR) or 'were eating' (PST of h₁édti)

english: A man was standing at the ford, and his name was Dog. Enemies were coming against him, and he killed ten, and the ford was red. Then they wounded him, and he grew tired. He said: 'I will not lie down. Standing I will die.' He leaned against the chariot. Then death came to him. They did not come near him and were trembling. Then an eagle came and sat on his head. Then they came near and cut off his head. The Dog's fame is great.
uncertain: moréyet: PST 'was killing / killed'
kʷékʷloy h₁épi: 'on/against the chariot'
h₃érō: 'eagle'

english: The serpent lay around the mountain and enclosed the waters. The earth dried up, the blossom withered, and the cattle were thirsty. The gods spoke to Perkunos: 'Perkunos, slay the serpent. Free the waters.' Drinking mead, Perkunos grew strong. He went to it and struck the serpent. The serpent rose up against him. Then Perkunos slew the serpent and split the mountain. The waters came forth from the mountain, and the rivers went to the sea. Then it rained. The cattle drank, the earth was fruitful, and the blossom came forth. The gods said: 'Perkunos, you who slew the serpent, who freed the waters, your fame is imperishable.'
uncertain: bʰérǵʰom: 'hill', read as 'mountain'
h₁éyt with déh₂nuh₂: 3SG verb with neuter plural subject
dʰéwgʰt: PST of dʰéwgʰti 'be productive' (vs AOR 'hit, meet')
gʷʰént: PST of gʷʰénti, read as completed 'slew'
h₂ékʷeh₂es: NOM.PL (vs GEN.SG)

english: The Light one (H₁lengʷhros) was swimming across the sea. He grew tired and sank in the water, and his heart trembled. Then he cried out to the sons of Sky: 'Sons of Sky, you two, rescue me. Death is before me.' Then the two heard him and yoked the swift horses to the chariot. The horses carried the chariot over the sea. Then the two pulled him out of the water and set him in the chariot. Then they carried him to his father. He (the father) saw him and rejoiced. He gave them ten horses, and their fame became great.
uncertain: h₁ln̥gʷʰrós: 'light' used as a name
suHnówbʰos / tóybʰos: DAT.PL for the two sons (no dual oblique form)
ḱlutā́m: AOR.3DU 'the two heard' (vs ACC of ḱlutós)
tóm kʷéḱt: subject taken as the father

english: Warriors were sitting around the king. They had captured cattle and a woman. Then the giver of good things (the king) spoke: 'She will be my woman.' Then Leudheros (the Free one) stood up and said: 'King, I took her with my spear. She will not be yours.' The king said to them: 'Seize that woman.' Then they seized her and led her to him. Then Leudheros went away to his own chariot and sat by the sea, and his tears were flowing. He spoke a word there: 'For the giver of good things I will not enter battle. May his warriors fall.' Then there was a great battle, and they grew cold (died). Leudheros sat in the chariot and did not lift a spear.
uncertain: h₁uséwōm déh₃tōr: 'giver of goods', epithet of the king
h₁pént: 'seized' (AOR) or 'were seizing'

studént: AOR.3PL 'grew cold' = died; subject inferred as the warriors

english: Keh₂ilos wanted to see the sun's chariot. He went along the sun's path. He walked for a year, and his nails split. He swam across waters and climbed hills. Then he reached the sea. The sun came up out of the water over there. The sun's chariot was burning, and its light was great. Keh₂ilos was astonished and spoke to the sun: 'Sun, where is my father?' The sun said: 'He is with the gods. He has drunk mead and is satisfied. Go to your mother. When you die, you will see him.' Then Keh₂ilos came to her and told her the sun's word, and the mother's heart grew warm.
uncertain: kéh₂ilos: 'whole' used as a name
yóh₁r̥: ACC of duration 'for a year'
h₂én: 'there, yonder'

english: A swift warrior was searching for his own father's cattle. Then he came to a great river. The river was in flood (full), its water had turned cold, and his horses trembled. Then he spoke to it: 'River, give me a path. I will give you poured mead.' Then he put mead into the water. The river slackened, and he found a ford. He led the horses across the ford. The cattle were grazing there. Then he drove the cattle across the ford and came to his father. He (the father) rejoiced and said: 'Dear one, I will give you a famous name, and your fame will be great.'
uncertain: pléh₁yos: comparative form 'fuller', read as 'full'
stéwdt-kʷe tósyo h₂ékʷeh₂: 'and its water became cold' - odd but grammatical
ǵʰutóm: participle 'poured (as libation)'
h₁dént: 'ate / were eating'
